questions.stem: Your lecture notes reduce the definition of general anesthesia to three core elements. Which set is it?
questions.explanation: The note states the definition as amnesia, unconsciousness, and immobility. The slide adds muscle relaxation and blunting of autonomic response as components.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: At skin incision, a patient with an adequate end-tidal sevoflurane does not move, but HR jumps from 72 to 118 and BP from 120/70 to 175/100. Which component of GA is inadequate?
questions.explanation: The patient is immobile and adequately hypnotized, but the sympathetic surge shows inadequate analgesia and autonomic blunting. An opioid is the usual fix.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: During an inhalation induction, a child becomes agitated, flails, and has irregular breathing with disconjugate gaze. Which stage is this?
questions.explanation: Stage 2 features disinhibition, uncontrolled movement, irregular respirations, hypersensitive airway reflexes, HTN/tachycardia, and disconjugate gaze.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: During a slow mask induction, a child develops irregular breathing, dilated pupils, and breath-holding. The resident wants to place an oral airway now. Why is this risky?
options: Stage 2 airway reflexes are hypersensitive, risking laryngospasm
Stage 2 relaxes the jaw too much for an oral airway
Stage 2 causes apnea that requires immediate intubation
Stage 2 lowers BP so far that airway insertion is unsafe
questions.explanation: The excitement stage brings hypersensitive airway reflexes; stimulating the airway now can trigger laryngospasm. Deepen first.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: Which findings place a patient in stage 3, surgical anesthesia? (Select 2)
options: Loss of eyelash and swallowing reflexes
Fixed, dilated pupils with medullary depression
Disorientation with intact reflexes and amnesia
questions.explanation: Stage 3 brings loss of reflexes and regular but depressed ventilation. Irregular breathing and movement are stage 2, disorientation with amnesia is stage 1, and fixed dilated pupils mark stage 4.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: During a long case, the vaporizer is accidentally left at 8% sevoflurane. The patient now has fixed, dilated pupils, BP 55/30, and no spontaneous effort. Which stage is this, and what is the action?
options: Stage 2; deepen further to blunt reflexes
questions.explanation: Fixed dilated pupils with medullary and cardiovascular depression mark stage 4, an overdose that requires stopping the agent and resuscitating.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: The notes point out that a patient under GA can do what?
questions.explanation: The notes say patients can spontaneously ventilate under GA, which is why GA is defined by unconsciousness, not by apnea.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: As a mask induction starts, the patient becomes confused, says the pain in her leg is gone, and later cannot recall the first minute. Reflexes are intact. Which stage was she in?
questions.explanation: Stage 1 brings analgesia, disorientation, and amnesia with intact reflexes and regular breathing.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: A patient has a T4 spinal for a cesarean, and another has GA with sevoflurane for a colectomy. Both are ready for incision. Which stage of anesthesia do both reflect for surgery?
questions.explanation: Stage 3 is surgical anesthesia, the target for surgery under GA or an adequate spinal.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: During emergence, a patient coughs violently and becomes hypertensive with the ETT still in. Which stage should you "beware" of here?
questions.explanation: Emergence passes back through stage 2, where reflexes are hypersensitive. The reflexes slide warns "beware stage 2."
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: A patient under sevoflurane does not move or respond to a sternal rub or incision and needs controlled ventilation. Where does this fall on the ASA continuum?
options: General anesthesia, unarousable even to painful stimuli
Deep sedation, responsive to repeated painful stimuli
questions.explanation: GA sits at the far end of the continuum because patients are unarousable even to painful stimulation.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: During emergence, a patient becomes hypertensive and tachycardic, breathes irregularly, and starts thrashing. Which stage is he passing through?
questions.explanation: Stage 2 brings hypertension, tachycardia, irregular breathing, and uncontrolled movement, at induction or emergence.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: A student describes stage 3 as "one level." How is stage 3 actually divided?
options: Into three planes of increasing depth
questions.explanation: Stage 3 contains four planes, from light surgical anesthesia to deep anesthesia approaching overdose.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: During stable stage 3 anesthesia with spontaneous ventilation through an LMA, ETCO2 rises from 40 to 52 while the breathing pattern stays smooth. What explains this?
options: Ventilation in stage 3 is regular but depressed
Ventilation in stage 3 is irregular with breath-holding
questions.explanation: Stage 3 ventilation is regular but depressed, so CO2 rises with deepening anesthesia.
questions.topic: Definition and stages of general anesthesia

questions.stem: The surgeon completed a full H&P in clinic 3 weeks ago. In preop today, the patient mentions new chest tightness since last week. What must the anesthesia provider do?
options: Review the H&P and determine what has changed
Accept the surgeon's H&P without review
Repeat a full H&P from the beginning
Repeat a full history and physical from scratch
questions.explanation: Even when another provider performed the assessment, you must review it and decide whether anything has changed. New chest tightness is exactly that kind of change.

questions.stem: Just before induction, you notice the consent is unsigned and the patient's BP is 210/115, new since yesterday. Which immediate pre-anesthesia items are failing? (Select 2)
options: Physiologic changes since the preop evaluation
The surgeon's case volume this month
questions.explanation: The immediate assessment confirms consent, site marking, ID, allergies, physiologic changes since preop, equipment, and antibiotic timing.

questions.stem: An intubated trauma patient on norepinephrine and receiving blood is brought straight from the ICU to the OR. Which handoff items are essential? (Select 4)
options: Report from the ICU nurse or team
Active drips, fluids, and blood products
Chart review of recent events and labs
A surgical time-out performed in the ICU
questions.explanation: Direct-to-OR patients need chart review, a report from the ICU team, active medications and products, and airway and ventilator parameters.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with CAD is about to be induced with propofol. How should you set the NIBP cycle during induction?
questions.explanation: NIBP should cycle every 2–3 minutes during induction, when hemodynamic swings are fastest.

questions.stem: Seconds after induction, a patient vomits. Your suction tubing is coiled on the machine and not connected. What standard was missed?
options: Suction turned on, connected, and within reach
Suction checked at the end of the case
questions.explanation: Suction must be on and within reach before every induction, because regurgitation can occur without warning.

questions.stem: You are setting up for a routine induction in a 65-year-old with hypertension. Which drugs should be drawn up and immediately available before induction?
questions.explanation: Keeping a vasopressor and succinylcholine out and ready covers the two most common early emergencies: hypotension and an airway crisis such as laryngospasm.

questions.stem: Before induction, which IV setup items must be confirmed? (Select 3)
options: A patent IV with fluids flowing
Pertinent drugs connected in the manifold
A central line for all GA cases
An arterial line for all GA cases
questions.explanation: The pre-induction check includes a patent IV, flowing fluids, cleaned ports, and drugs in the manifold.

questions.stem: After moving a patient onto the OR table, you notice the ECG cable is under her back and one arm is hanging off the board. What should you correct before induction?
options: Support both arms and remove wires from under the patient
Tuck both arms at the sides for every case
Remove the pillow for the best laryngoscopy view
Raise the legs to increase venous return
questions.explanation: Arms should be supported and the patient should not lie on wires or equipment, which can cause pressure injury.

questions.stem: During a case, the patient desaturates for 2 minutes before anyone notices, because the SpO2 alarm volume was turned to zero. Which immediate assessment item was missed?
questions.explanation: The immediate assessment requires equipment checks with alarms on and audible.

questions.stem: Two patients named John Smith are in preop. One has a penicillin allergy. Scanning the ID band confirms which items?
options: Identity, date of birth, and allergies
NPO time and last medication dose
questions.explanation: Scanning the ID band confirms identity, DOB, and allergies, preventing wrong-patient errors.

questions.stem: A patient's chart weight is 90 kg from 6 months ago, but she has since lost 25 kg. You plan rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg. What dose difference results from using the old weight?
options: 108 mg versus 78 mg, about 30 mg too much
90 mg versus 65 mg, about 25 mg too much
120 mg versus 90 mg, about 30 mg too much
No difference, since rocuronium is not weight based
questions.explanation: 1.2 × 90 = 108 mg; 1.2 × 65 = 78 mg. Current weight matters because drug dosing depends on it.

questions.stem: Special Scenario #1 describes transport from the ICU. Which element shows ventilation was maintained?
options: 100% O2 via Ambu to ETT with adequate chest rise
Nasal cannula at 4 L/min during the transport
questions.explanation: The documentation describes 100% O2 via Ambu to ETT with manual ventilation and adequate chest rise on full ASA monitors.

questions.stem: You set up for a routine GA with an ETT. Which airway setup is required before induction?
options: Primary device, backup airway, and video or emergency aids
Primary device, with backup kept in the hallway
A video laryngoscope for known difficult airways
A cricothyrotomy kit opened on the field
questions.explanation: Pre-induction setup requires a primary device, backup airway, and video or emergency adjuncts for every case.

questions.stem: After propofol 200 mg, BP falls to 60/30 and you have to draw up phenylephrine from scratch. Which preparation would have prevented the delay? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Induction agents, emergency vasopressors, and adjuncts must be ready before induction.

questions.stem: The oxygen pipeline fails just as you begin preoxygenation. Which pre-induction check should have confirmed you could still deliver oxygen?
options: Nitrous oxide as a backup gas
questions.explanation: Pre-induction setup confirms high-flow 100% O2, including the backup cylinder.

questions.stem: A patient arrives from the ED directly to the OR with a trauma. What must still be reviewed?
options: Chart, report, active drugs, airway, and vent settings
The last set of labs and the surgical consent
Nothing further if the ED physician intubated
questions.explanation: Direct-to-OR patients still need chart review, report, active medications and products, and airway/ventilatory review.

questions.stem: You are preparing monitors for an elective induction. Which setup is correct?
options: ASA monitors, NIBP every 2–3 minutes, and O2 and gas analysis
ASA monitors, NIBP every 5 minutes, and SpO2 until intubation
ECG and SpO2, with NIBP started after incision
ASA monitors plus processed EEG for every case
questions.explanation: Pre-induction setup includes ASA standard monitors, frequent NIBP, and oxygen and gas analysis.

questions.stem: A patient is induced before the site is marked, and the surgeon begins prepping the wrong knee. Which risk does site confirmation prevent?
questions.explanation: Confirming site marking before induction prevents wrong-site surgery, since the patient cannot verify once asleep.

questions.stem: A patient's BP has risen to 190/110 since the preop visit yesterday. What does the immediate assessment require?
options: Recognize the change and reassess before induction
Proceed because the preop visit was normal
Proceed and treat the change after incision
Proceed unless the patient reports symptoms
questions.explanation: Physiologic changes since the preoperative evaluation must be identified before induction.

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, the gas analyzer shows expired O2 rising. At what end-tidal O2 is denitrogenation nearly complete?
questions.explanation: Denitrogenation is nearly complete at an EtO2 of about 90%.

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, the EtO2 plateaus at 72% despite 3 minutes of tidal breathing. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Mask leak preventing a tight seal
Oxygen consumption that is too low
questions.explanation: Mask leaks and dead space limit preoxygenation. A plateau well below 90% suggests entrained room air.

questions.stem: You are preoxygenating a patient for an RSI and want the highest possible FiO2 at the mask. What fresh gas flow should you use?
questions.explanation: Maximum FiO2 requires fresh gas flows above 10 L/min, which also prevents dilution with room air.

questions.stem: A cooperative patient will be preoxygenated with normal breathing. Which technique is correct?
options: Tight mask with 100% O2 above 10 L/min for 3–5 minutes
Loose mask with 50% O2 for 1 minute
Nasal cannula at 4 L/min for 10 minutes before induction
Room air with deep breaths for 5 minutes
questions.explanation: Passive preoxygenation uses a tight-fitting mask with 100% O2 above 10 L/min for 3–5 minutes of tidal breathing.

questions.stem: Which patients will desaturate faster during apnea because of a reduced FRC? (Select 4)
options: A patient with a BMI of 45
A cirrhotic patient with tense ascites
A healthy adult in reverse Trendelenburg
questions.explanation: FRC is reduced with obesity, late pregnancy, ascites, pediatrics, and the elderly. Head-up positioning increases FRC.

questions.stem: Two patients are preoxygenated identically. One has a large FRC, the other a small one. How does the large FRC affect the process?
options: It takes longer to fill but delays desaturation
It fills faster and shortens time to desaturation
It fills faster and shortens safe apnea time
It changes neither the filling time nor desaturation time
questions.explanation: A larger FRC takes longer to denitrogenate but holds a bigger oxygen reservoir, prolonging safe apnea time.

questions.stem: A patient with a BMI of 48 desaturates quickly during a prior induction. How should you position her this time to improve FRC?
questions.explanation: Ramping and reverse Trendelenburg shift abdominal contents away from the diaphragm and increase FRC.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient desaturates quickly during apnea. Which two factors explain this?
options: Decreased FRC and increased O2 consumption
Increased FRC and decreased O2 consumption
Decreased dead space and increased FRC
Increased cardiac output and lower V/Q mismatch
questions.explanation: Late pregnancy decreases FRC and increases O2 consumption, both speeding desaturation.

questions.stem: A preoxygenated patient becomes apneic. At what approximate rate is oxygen consumed from the FRC reservoir?
questions.explanation: Oxygen consumption is about 250 mL/min in adults, which determines how long the FRC reservoir lasts.

questions.stem: During a difficult intubation in an obese patient, a nasal cannula at 15 L/min is left on during apnea. SpO2 stays above 95% for 6 minutes. What is this technique doing?
options: Ventilating the patient and removing CO2
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation keeps the FRC filled with oxygen by mass flow during apnea, delaying desaturation. It does not remove CO2.

questions.stem: Which patients should get apneic oxygenation during intubation? (Select 4)
options: A patient with a BMI of 48
A patient with a predicted difficult airway
A patient undergoing rapid sequence intubation
A healthy ASA I adult with an easy airway
A patient with low oxygen consumption at rest
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation is recommended for obesity, pregnancy, lung disease, predicted difficult airway, low reserve, and RSI.

questions.stem: Which patient is MOST likely to benefit from apneic oxygenation because of intrinsic lung disease?
options: A patient with mild intermittent asthma
A healthy patient with a resolved pneumonia
A patient with remote treated TB
questions.explanation: Intrinsic lung disease such as COPD and pulmonary fibrosis shortens safe apnea time and is an indication for apneic oxygenation.

questions.stem: Which patients will make a tight mask seal harder during preoxygenation? (Select 4)
options: A man with a full beard
A patient with a nasogastric tube
A patient with a facial deformity
questions.explanation: Mask seal is compromised by edentulousness, facial hair, an NGT, and facial deformity.

questions.stem: An obese patient's EtO2 stalls at 80% with tidal breathing on a tight mask. You add CPAP of 10 cmH2O, and EtO2 reaches 90%. What type of preoxygenation is this?
questions.explanation: Active preoxygenation uses positive pressure such as CPAP or NIV to recruit lung and increase FRC.

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, adding 5–10 cmH2O PEEP speeds EtO2 rise and lengthens safe apnea time in an obese patient. Why?
options: PEEP increases FRC by recruiting collapsed alveoli
PEEP lowers FiO2 to a safer level
PEEP lowers oxygen consumption during apnea
questions.explanation: PEEP recruits alveoli, increasing FRC and the oxygen reservoir.

questions.stem: You plan high-flow nasal oxygen for preoxygenation. What limitation should you expect?
options: Uncertain FiO2 and EtO2 measurement, plus gastric insufflation
It delivers a fixed, known FiO2 at all flows
It requires a tight-fitting mask seal
Its flow is capped well below peak inspiratory flow rates
questions.explanation: HFNO makes FiO2 and EtO2 hard to measure and can insufflate the stomach.

questions.stem: A colleague suggests using nasal cannula alone instead of the circuit mask for preoxygenation. How do they compare?
options: Nasal options help but are less effective than a mask on the circuit
Nasal options are superior to a mask on the circuit
Nasal options are required for every RSI
Nasal options are equivalent to a tight mask at high flow
questions.explanation: Nasal techniques can supplement oxygenation, but a tight mask on the circuit remains more effective for preoxygenation.

questions.stem: What causes absorption atelectasis during preoxygenation?
options: Alveolar collapse as oxygen is absorbed
Nitrogen accumulation in alveoli after preoxygenation
questions.explanation: Absorption atelectasis occurs when oxygen is absorbed and alveoli collapse after denitrogenation.

questions.stem: After 30 minutes of 100% O2 following induction, a CT shows atelectasis in dependent lung regions. Which strategies reduce this? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Lowering FiO2 below 1.0, adding PEEP, and recruitment maneuvers reduce absorption atelectasis.

questions.stem: During a prolonged difficult airway, apneic oxygenation keeps SpO2 at 96% for 10 minutes. The first ABG after intubation shows pH 7.12 and PaCO2 88. What explains this?
options: CO2 rose about 3–6 mmHg per minute without ventilation
The SpO2 reading was falsely high
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation maintains oxygenation but not ventilation; CO2 accumulates, causing respiratory acidosis.

questions.stem: During a prolonged intubation with apneic oxygenation, SpO2 stays 98% but ETCO2 is 68 on the first breath. What explains this?
options: Ventilation by the apneic patient maintained oxygenation
questions.explanation: Oxygen can reach alveoli without breathing, but CO2 elimination requires ventilation. Apnea causes hypercarbia even when SpO2 is normal.

questions.stem: During preoxygenation with CPAP in an obese patient, the abdomen becomes distended. What risk does this create?
options: Gastric insufflation with regurgitation and aspiration risk
Hypocarbia with seizures from hyperventilation by CPAP
questions.explanation: Positive airway pressure can insufflate the stomach, raising regurgitation and aspiration risk.

questions.stem: Two patients are preoxygenated identically: a healthy 40-year-old and a febrile patient with septic shock. The septic patient desaturates within 90 seconds of apnea. What MOST explains this?
questions.explanation: Sepsis increases oxygen consumption, which empties the FRC oxygen reservoir faster.

questions.stem: A patient needs RSI but can only tolerate 1 minute of mask breathing. Which technique gives the best preoxygenation in a short time?
options: Nasal cannula at 4 L/min for 1 minute
questions.explanation: Vital capacity breaths with a tight mask rapidly denitrogenate the lungs, a good alternative to 3 minutes of tidal breathing.

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, an obese patient's EtO2 stalls because of partial obstruction. You tell her to "point your chin to the ceiling." What does this achieve?
questions.explanation: Chin lift and head extension open the airway, improving gas flow during preoxygenation.

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia and 30% shunt has EtO2 of 90% after preoxygenation, but SpO2 is only 91%. Why does high FiO2 not fully correct his oxygenation?
options: His oxygen consumption is too low
His mask seal is too tight
questions.explanation: With shunt, blood passes through unventilated lung and cannot pick up oxygen regardless of FiO2.

questions.stem: A colleague plans standard nasal cannula at 5 L/min as the only preoxygenation for an RSI. Why is this inadequate?
options: Flow and FiO2 are too low to fully denitrogenate
Nasal cannula causes gastric insufflation at any flow
Nasal cannula is contraindicated in RSI
questions.explanation: Standard nasal cannula cannot deliver high enough flow or FiO2 for effective preoxygenation.

questions.stem: A bearded patient with a nasogastric tube needs an RSI. After 3 minutes on the mask, EtO2 is only 65%. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.explanation: A beard and an NGT both prevent a tight seal, so room air dilutes the delivered oxygen.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old desaturates faster than a 40-year-old after identical preoxygenation. Which age-related change contributes?
questions.explanation: FRC and oxygen reserve decrease with age, and closing capacity rises, shortening safe apnea time.

questions.stem: You choose an IV induction for a 40-year-old with prior PONV. Which advantages support this choice? (Select 4)
options: Rapid onset that suits RSI needs
Maintains spontaneous ventilation with an airway mass
Preferred when IV access is difficult
questions.explanation: IV induction offers rapid onset, suits RSI, causes less PONV, has no odor, and is easily titrated. Inhalational induction preserves spontaneous ventilation and suits patients without IV access.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: A patient has a large anterior mediastinal mass and airway compression. Why might inhalation induction be preferred?
questions.explanation: Inhalation induction is useful when maintaining spontaneous ventilation is desirable, as with airway stenosis or mass.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: Which patients are good candidates for inhalation induction? (Select 4)
options: A patient with no IV access after multiple attempts
A patient with a tracheostomy already in place
A patient with an airway mass who must keep spontaneous ventilation
A patient with a full stomach needing RSI
An adult with easy IV access and no special needs
questions.explanation: Inhalation induction suits children, fearful patients, difficult IV access, an in situ airway, and the need to maintain spontaneous ventilation.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: You are planning a standard IV induction for a healthy adult. Roughly how long does it take from drug to readiness for airway placement?
questions.explanation: A normal induction averages about 3 minutes.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: You are performing an RSI for a patient with a bowel obstruction. What is the target time from induction to a secured airway?
questions.explanation: RSI aims to secure the airway in under 60 seconds to limit the unprotected period.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with a small bowel obstruction is vomiting. You plan propofol and succinylcholine back-to-back, then intubate without mask ventilation. Which features define this technique? (Select 2)
options: Full stomach or high aspiration risk
It is limited to elective cases
Planned LMA placement as the first device
questions.explanation: RSI assumes a full stomach and uses a rapid drug sequence without routine mask ventilation, aiming for a cuffed ETT.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: In a routine elective induction, you confirm mask ventilation before giving rocuronium. Why is this possible in a normal induction but not an RSI?
options: The slower sequence leaves time to assess ventilation
Aspiration risk is negligible in elective cases
Rocuronium has a slower onset than succinylcholine
Mask ventilation is not needed in RSI
questions.explanation: A normal induction proceeds more slowly, allowing confirmation of mask ventilation before paralysis.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: During an RSI for a full-stomach patient, which airway device is avoided as the primary airway?
options: An oral airway for brief mask support
questions.explanation: An LMA does not protect against aspiration, so RSI aims for a cuffed ETT.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with an incarcerated hernia needs an RSI. Which premedications are appropriate? (Select 3)
options: GI medications to reduce acid and volume
Atropine if bradycardia is a concern
questions.explanation: RSI premedication can include anxiolytics, GI medications, atropine, and preoxygenation.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: During an RSI in a 4-year-old, why might atropine be ready?
options: Atropine blocks laryngospasm triggered by secretions
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine can cause bradycardia, especially in children and with repeat dosing, so atropine is kept available.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: An awake patient with a bowel obstruction is about to receive cricoid pressure before induction. Which force is appropriate, and what does it feel like?
options: About 10 N, roughly 1 kg of pressure
About 30 N, roughly 3 kg of pressure
About 50 N, roughly 5 kg of pressure
About 100 N, roughly 10 kg of pressure
questions.explanation: About 10 N (about 1 kg) is tolerable awake; it increases to about 30 N (3 kg) after loss of consciousness.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: What cricoid pressure force is recommended after the patient is asleep?
questions.explanation: Cricoid pressure increases to about 30 N once asleep.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: During cricoid pressure, the assistant pushes the larynx up and to the left. What is the correct technique?
options: Press the cricoid backward against the vertebrae
Push the thyroid cartilage to the right
Press the cricoid upward toward the chin
Squeeze the trachea from both sides
questions.explanation: Cricoid pressure compresses the esophagus by pressing the cricoid ring backward against the cervical vertebrae.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: During an RSI, an assistant applies cricoid pressure and your laryngoscopic view is grade III. Which risks of cricoid pressure are relevant here? (Select 2)
options: More difficult laryngoscopy and mask ventilation
A better view in most cases
questions.explanation: Cricoid pressure can worsen laryngoscopy and ventilation, prolong intubation, and cause hoarseness, and its benefit is questionable.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: During an RSI, mask ventilation becomes impossible after cricoid pressure is applied. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: Cricoid pressure can occlude the airway
Cricoid pressure reliably prevents aspiration in this setting
questions.explanation: Cricoid pressure can occlude the airway and may not help, so easing it is reasonable if ventilation or the view suffers.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: A patient with a full stomach and severe COPD desaturates rapidly. You plan an RSI but allow gentle mask breaths before intubation. What is this called?
options: RSI using an LMA as the primary device
questions.explanation: A modified RSI adjusts the classic technique, often allowing gentle mask ventilation in patients who cannot tolerate apnea.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: You are about to perform an RSI on a patient with a small mouth opening and a full stomach. Which preparation step is essential?
options: Backup emergency airway equipment in the room
Neuromuscular reversal drawn up in advance
A TIVA pump ready for maintenance
questions.explanation: RSI preparation includes airway evaluation, backup emergency airway equipment, premedication, and positioning.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with SBO needs emergency laparotomy. Which induction type is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: SBO means full stomach and high aspiration risk, requiring RSI.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: A trauma patient with a full stomach also has a short neck and limited mouth opening. How do these findings relate?
options: RSI cases often come with predicted airway difficulty
RSI is reserved for airways predicted to be easy
questions.explanation: Emergency and full-stomach conditions often coexist with predicted airway difficulty, so backup plans are essential.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: A patient with CAD needs an IV induction, and you want to prevent a large hemodynamic surge at laryngoscopy. What is the role of adjuvants?
questions.explanation: Adjuvants such as opioids, lidocaine, or esmolol blunt the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: Before RSI in a pregnant patient, you give 30 mL of sodium citrate. Why?
options: Nonparticulate antacid that raises gastric pH
H2 blocker that reduces acid production
questions.explanation: Sodium citrate (Bicitra) is a nonparticulate antacid that reduces lung injury if aspiration occurs.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: For a cooperative adult with an IV in place, which induction route is MOST common?
questions.explanation: IV induction is most common in adults; inhalation induction is most common in children and uncooperative patients.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: Which induction choice is MOST appropriate for a 4-year-old without IV access for tonsillectomy?
questions.explanation: Inhalation induction is used in peds and with difficult IV access.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: During a classic RSI, why don't you test mask ventilation before giving succinylcholine?
options: No time, and it can insufflate the stomach
Cricoid pressure makes mask ventilation ineffective
The ETT is already in place
questions.explanation: RSI minimizes the time between loss of reflexes and intubation and avoids gastric insufflation from positive pressure.
questions.topic: Induction options, RSI, and cricoid pressure

questions.stem: After propofol and rocuronium, you are mask ventilating. Which signs show the patient is ready for an advanced airway? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Readiness signs include loss of lash reflex, jaw relaxation, apnea, compliant mask ventilation, and adequate time for drug onset.

questions.stem: You give propofol and rocuronium and attempt laryngoscopy 30 seconds later. The patient coughs and bucks. What principle was missed?
options: Drugs need time to reach peak effect before laryngoscopy
The surgeon sets the timing of intubation
Intubation must occur within 10 seconds of induction
questions.explanation: Instrumenting before drugs peak risks coughing, laryngospasm, and hemodynamic surges.

questions.stem: After intubation you see a capnogram waveform. How many breaths of sustained ETCO2 should you see to confirm placement?
questions.explanation: Confirmation includes sustained capnography for six breaths with bilateral breath sounds, chest rise, and fog.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram G. Right after intubation, the waveform fades to zero over five breaths while SpO2 is still 97%. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.explanation: CO2 from swallowed air can appear briefly and then fade. Sustained capnography for six breaths is required to confirm tracheal placement.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram G. After intubation, you see a few small waveforms that rapidly fall to zero, while SpO2 starts to drop. What is the BEST next step?
options: Remove the ETT, mask ventilate, and reattempt
Leave the ETT and increase the tidal volume
questions.explanation: Waveforms that disappear after a few breaths suggest esophageal intubation; remove the tube, oxygenate, and reattempt.

questions.stem: You have just placed an ETT. Which findings confirm tracheal placement? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Confirmation uses bilateral breath sounds, sustained ETCO2, bilateral chest rise, and fog. One ETCO2 reading can come from the stomach.

questions.stem: After intubation, breath sounds are present only on the right and peak pressure is high. What is the MOST likely problem?
questions.explanation: Mainstem intubation typically goes right and causes unilateral breath sounds and high pressures.

questions.stem: Immediately after induction and intubation, which complications should you be ready to recognize? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Post-induction complications include bronchospasm, laryngospasm, aspiration, misplaced airway, dental injury, a poorly fitting SGA, anaphylaxis, and MH.

questions.stem: After induction and intubation, what belongs in your post-induction assessment? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Post-induction assessment covers CV status, respiratory status, depth, and early complications.

questions.stem: Special Scenario #2 documents which detail of the difficult intubation?
options: Attempts by each provider with view grade
The name of the attending who intubated
questions.explanation: The documentation lists mask ventilation difficulty, each attempt with grade, ETT size, depth, blade, confirmation, and no trauma.

questions.stem: After three attempts by two providers, the airway is secured with a VL and bougie. Why document the number of attempts and who made each?
options: It is required for the quality database alone
questions.explanation: Documenting attempts, operators, views, and devices tells future providers what worked and what didn't.

questions.stem: You place an ETT and immediately tape it before checking ETCO2. Which statements about securing the airway are correct? (Select 2)
options: Secure the tube before confirming placement
questions.explanation: Confirm placement first, then secure the airway and document the depth at the lip or teeth.

questions.stem: Why is suction on and readily accessible during airway management?
options: Secretions, blood, or vomit may need immediate clearing
It improves oxygen delivery during apnea
It prevents bradycardia from laryngoscopy and suction
It confirms ETT placement after intubation
questions.explanation: Suction must be ready to clear secretions or regurgitation during induction.

questions.stem: Why is an oral airway useful during mask ventilation?
options: It relieves tongue obstruction to improve mask ventilation
It confirms tracheal placement of the ETT after intubation
It replaces jaw thrust in most patients
questions.explanation: An OA helps maintain airway patency when the tongue obstructs.

questions.stem: During a laparoscopy with an LMA, peak pressure is 24, you hear a loud leak, and exhaled tidal volume is half the set volume. What is the problem?
questions.explanation: A poorly fitting SGA leaks, delivering inadequate tidal volumes, especially with raised abdominal pressure.

questions.stem: Which damage should be assessed after intubation?
options: Teeth, lips, and oral or nasal structures
The trachea below the vocal cords
questions.explanation: Accidental damage to teeth, lips, and oral/nasal structures is listed.

questions.stem: A patient becomes difficult to ventilate after induction with wheezing. Which post-induction complication is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Wheezing and high pressures after induction suggest bronchospasm.

questions.stem: After induction for a 40-minute knee arthroscopy in a fasted healthy patient, what airway decision do you make next?
questions.explanation: After induction, you choose between an SGA and an ETT based on aspiration risk, surgery, and positioning.

questions.stem: After intubation, you see condensation appear and clear inside the ETT with each breath. What does this indicate, and how reliable is it?
questions.explanation: Fog shows humidified gas moving through the tube, but it can occur with esophageal placement, so capnography is required.

questions.stem: After two failed laryngoscopy attempts, the patient is still mask ventilating but with effort. Which questions should guide the next step? (Select 3)
options: Who should make the next attempt?
Does the airway device or technique need to change?
What ETT size does the surgeon prefer?
Which blade does the patient prefer?
When is the antibiotic due for redosing?
questions.explanation: Multiple attempts raise concerns about mask ventilation, who manages each attempt, whether to change the airway type, and what would make success more likely.

questions.stem: A patient reports hearing the surgeon say "start closing" and feeling the tube in her throat, but no pain. What type of awareness is this?
questions.explanation: Explicit recall is conscious memory of intraoperative events due to inadequate hypnosis.

questions.stem: After surgery, a patient has no memory of the procedure, but she becomes anxious whenever she hears a phrase spoken during the case. What does this suggest?
options: Explicit recall of events during the case
questions.explanation: Implicit memory influences behavior or emotion without conscious recall of the event.

questions.stem: A patient reports recall of voices and paralysis during her prior surgery. Which psychological effects is she at risk for? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Awareness can cause anxiety, PTSD, nightmares, and ongoing distress.

questions.stem: A patient reports explicit recall of her surgery. What are your ethical responsibilities? (Select 3)
options: Document the complication in the record
Disclose promptly and discuss what happened
Follow up with options to reduce future risk
Wait for the patient to raise it again
Refer her to legal counsel only
questions.explanation: Awareness requires documentation, prompt disclosure, and follow-up with options to reduce future risk.

questions.stem: During induction, what causes the awareness risk gap?
options: Loss of responsiveness before adequate depth is reached
Excess depth before laryngoscopy causing hypotension
questions.explanation: The gap between loss of responsiveness and adequate depth creates awareness risk.

questions.stem: Which factors increase awareness risk during induction? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: RSI and difficult airways raise awareness risk because hypnotic dosing may lapse during intubation. Volatile anesthesia with ETAG monitoring lowers risk.

questions.stem: Which maintenance patients carry higher risk of awareness? (Select 4)
options: A woman having an emergency cesarean under GA
A hypotensive trauma patient receiving minimal anesthetic
A patient on propofol TIVA with paralysis
A patient who had awareness during a prior anesthetic
An ASA I outpatient on sevoflurane with ETAG monitoring
A patient breathing spontaneously without NMB
questions.explanation: Higher awareness risk includes obstetrics, trauma, TIVA with paralysis, unstable patients, and those with prior awareness.

questions.stem: Which measures reduce awareness risk during maintenance? (Select 3)
options: Higher volatile concentrations in every patient
questions.explanation: Reduced risk with BIS, ETAG monitoring, avoiding NMB, and assessing clinical signs.

questions.stem: At the end of a case, the vaporizer is turned off while TOF is 0/4 and you wait for reversal. Why does this create awareness risk?
options: Depth is falling while paralysis still hides movement
Vaporizers keep delivering agent after being turned off
questions.explanation: Lowering depth while the patient is still paralyzed creates a window of awareness without movement to warn you.

questions.stem: The note on the awareness slide says which cause is common during induction?
questions.explanation: The note says induction awareness often comes from not enough medication.

questions.stem: Which team behaviors are expected during induction? (Select 3)
options: Anesthesia timeout with plan A and B
Discussion of the next case to save time
questions.explanation: Induction is a critical phase with no distractions, a timeout, plan A/B, and clear roles.

questions.stem: Before an RSI, you tell the team: "Plan A is VL with a bougie; if two attempts fail, I'll place an LMA. Watch for SpO2 below 90%." What does this build?
questions.explanation: A shared mental model means everyone knows the plan, expectations, and cues for complications.

questions.stem: During a difficult intubation, you say, "Bougie please." Which reply completes closed-loop communication?
questions.explanation: Closed-loop communication confirms the request, the action, and the result.

questions.stem: As an SRNA inducing your first patient, you say aloud, "Propofol 150 given, starting mask ventilation, rocuronium 50 in." Why is this practice valuable?
options: It keeps the team informed and allows early correction
It slows induction to prevent awareness
It replaces the need for written documentation later
It replaces the need for a written record
questions.explanation: Calling out drugs, doses, and steps keeps the team aligned and lets a preceptor catch errors in real time.

questions.stem: Which statement is the BEST example of speaking up during induction?
options: "I can't ventilate despite repositioning and an OA."
"Ventilation is a little hard, but let's continue."
"I'll give it a minute and see if it improves."
"I think the surgeon should decide what to do."
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes voicing concerns immediately with specific details.

questions.stem: What does "use proper terminology" mean during induction?
options: Use clear clinical terms like "grade I view"
Use casual language to reduce the patient's anxiety
Use local slang the team understands
questions.explanation: Proper anesthetic terminology improves clarity, such as describing the laryngoscopic grade.

questions.stem: During the anesthesia timeout before an RSI, what should be confirmed? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: The timeout confirms plan A and B, drug doses and sequence, the airway plan, and emergency equipment.

questions.stem: During induction, a nurse asks you about the next case while you are giving drugs and SpO2 drops. Why is induction treated as a critical phase?
options: Rapid changes need focus and roles
Induction is the longest phase of anesthesia
Induction has the lowest complication rate
questions.explanation: Induction brings rapid changes in airway and hemodynamics, so distractions must be minimized.

questions.stem: What should a novice request during difficult mask ventilation?
options: An LMA before trying any adjunct
A change in the surgical plan
questions.explanation: Requests like two-person ventilation or cricoid pressure are examples in the closed-loop slide.

questions.stem: You have just intubated a patient, confirmed ETCO2, and BP has stabilized after induction. Which phase begins now?
questions.explanation: Maintenance begins after induction, airway establishment, and stabilization.

questions.stem: Three minutes before incision, the patient's BIS is 58 on 0.8 MAC sevoflurane. Why deepen anesthesia now?
options: To blunt the response to incision
questions.explanation: Incision is intensely stimulating, so depth is increased beforehand to prevent movement, awareness, and hemodynamic surges.

questions.stem: You have just secured the airway for a 3-hour colectomy. Which are goals of the maintenance phase? (Select 4)
options: Muscle relaxation when surgery needs it
Fixed vaporizer settings for the whole case
questions.explanation: Maintenance goals include stage III anesthesia, analgesia, homeostasis, vigilance, and relaxation when needed.

questions.stem: During a hip replacement, anesthetic needs rise at incision, fall during cementing, and change again with 1.2 L blood loss. What concept does this illustrate?
options: Requirements change with stimulation but not physiology
questions.explanation: Anesthetic requirements change with stimulation, physiology, and blood loss throughout maintenance.

questions.stem: During maintenance, ETCO2 rises. You check the ventilator, increase the rate, recheck ETCO2, think ahead to closure, and chart the change. Which framework did you follow?
questions.explanation: The maintenance mental model is assess, interpret, intervene, reassess, anticipate, and document.

questions.stem: A patient later disputes that he received antibiotics, and the record shows nothing, although you remember giving cefazolin. What principle applies?
options: The circulator's record is enough to confirm
questions.explanation: Undocumented actions cannot be shown to have occurred.

questions.stem: After a prone repositioning for a spine case, which airway checks are priorities? (Select 3)
options: Recheck the ETT after positioning or table movement
Confirm the airway once at induction
questions.explanation: Post-induction airway priority includes waveform ETCO2, rechecking after movement, documenting depth, and keeping suction available.

questions.stem: After turning the patient prone, SpO2 falls and peak pressure rises. What is the FIRST step?
options: Recheck airway position and circuit integrity
Increase FiO2 and continue the case
Deepen the volatile agent to reduce airway reactivity
questions.explanation: The airway must be rechecked after positioning or table movement.

questions.stem: During maintenance, SpO2 falls to 88%. A novice reaches for the machine settings first. Which order should the novice approach follow?
options: Check the machine first, then the patient
Call for help before any assessment
Change the pulse oximeter probe first
questions.explanation: The novice approach to desaturation starts with the patient, then the airway, then the machine.

questions.stem: What does "oxygenation is more than SpO2" mean?
options: Normal SpO2 on high FiO2 can hide lung dysfunction
SpO2 reflects ventilation as well as oxygenation
questions.explanation: High FiO2 can maintain SpO2 despite worsening V/Q mismatch or shunt.

questions.stem: During a laparoscopy, SpO2 falls to 89%. Using the advanced approach, put these checks in order: O2 supply, airway, patient, monitor, ventilation/circuit.
options: Monitor, O2 supply, patient, airway, circuit
Airway, patient, monitor, circuit, O2 supply
O2 supply, monitor, circuit, airway, patient
questions.explanation: The advanced approach goes patient, airway, ventilation and circuit, O2 supply, then monitor.

questions.stem: During maintenance, SpO2 falls from 98% to 90%. Which are common causes to consider? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Causes include atelectasis, endobronchial intubation, bronchospasm, pneumothorax, aspiration, edema, embolism, and low cardiac output.

questions.stem: During which events in a case should you anticipate desaturation?
questions.explanation: Positioning, pneumoperitoneum, and one-lung ventilation are predictable times for desaturation during maintenance.

questions.stem: What does "treat the physiology, not the SpO2 value" mean?
options: Treat the cause, such as recruitment or PEEP
Raise FiO2 alone until SpO2 normalizes
Replace the pulse oximeter probe first
Deepen the volatile to reduce O2 demand
questions.explanation: Treatment should target the underlying physiology.

questions.stem: During a case, the patient's minute ventilation falls and a hissing sound comes from the circuit. Which check would have prevented this?
options: A leak test before every case
A daily machine check at the start of the day
A leak test when alarms sound
questions.explanation: A leak test before every case identifies circuit leaks before they affect ventilation.

questions.stem: During a long case, you do an ABCDE sweep. Which components does it include? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: ABCDE covers airway, breathing, circulation, drugs and depth, and equipment and environment.

questions.stem: During your ABCDE sweep, you reach "E." Which equipment checks belong there? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The equipment check covers circuit, gas, pumps, alarms, temperature, absorbent, ventilator, vaporizer, suction, warming, and emergency equipment.

questions.stem: During a Whipple, you draw up blood products before the vascular dissection and start a longer-acting opioid an hour before closure. Which mental model step is this?
questions.explanation: Anticipating means preparing for what is coming next rather than only reacting.

questions.stem: The NIBP suddenly reads 68/34 while HR, ETCO2, and SpO2 waveform are unchanged. What is the FIRST step?
questions.explanation: The hemodynamic slide says first confirm BP measurement accuracy, then assess the rest of the picture.

questions.stem: During maintenance, BP falls to 78/40. Which mechanisms should you consider? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Hypotension can come from vasodilation, hypovolemia or hemorrhage, myocardial depression, dysrhythmia, obstruction, anaphylaxis, or sympathectomy.

questions.stem: Two hours into a knee replacement, HR rises from 70 to 110 and BP from 120/70 to 165/95. Before deepening anesthesia, which causes should you consider? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Do not assume light anesthesia. Consider pain, inadequate hypnosis, hypercarbia, hypoxemia, bladder distention, tourniquet, withdrawal, and hyperthermia.

questions.stem: During TIVA, BP rises to 180/100 and HR to 115. Before treating "light anesthesia," what should you check first?
options: That drug is reaching the patient
That the patient's temperature is normal
That the urine output is adequate
questions.explanation: Confirm anesthetic delivery and IV patency first; an infiltrated or disconnected line causes light anesthesia and awareness.

questions.stem: During a case, BP falls to 75/40. Two phenylephrine doses and a fluid bolus produce only brief improvement, and you cannot find a cause. What is the BEST next step?
options: Place advanced monitoring, such as an arterial line
Increase the volatile to reduce stress response
questions.explanation: Persistent, unexplained, or treatment-resistant instability warrants advanced monitoring.

questions.stem: Which items belong in the surgical time-out? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: The time-out confirms patient, procedure, site, consent, position, allergies, antibiotics, blood, equipment, imaging, fire risk, and anesthesia concerns.

questions.stem: During the time-out, the circulator has not confirmed the implants, but the surgeon picks up the scalpel. What does "hard stop" require?
options: No incision until every team member confirms
The surgeon may proceed if he confirms
The anesthesia provider may override the stop
The time-out can be completed after incision
questions.explanation: A hard stop means no incision until the entire team confirms the time-out items.

questions.stem: What are typical signs of bronchospasm during maintenance? (Select 2)
options: A downsloping capnogram with low peak pressure
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm raises peak pressure and prolongs expiration with wheeze, producing an upsloping shark-fin capnogram.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram D. After intubation in an asthmatic patient, the capnogram shows a steep upslope without a plateau and PIP rises to 40. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: A shark-fin upslope with high PIP indicates expiratory obstruction such as bronchospasm.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram D. The patient was just repositioned with rising stimulation. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.explanation: Your notes say bronchospasm during maintenance is usually from surgical stimulation or light anesthesia.

questions.stem: After intubation, peak pressures rise to 42 with wheezing and a shark-fin capnogram. What is the BEST initial treatment?
options: Increase FiO2 and deepen anesthesia with propofol
Give esmolol and continue the volatile
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm is treated by raising FiO2, deepening anesthesia (propofol acts fastest), giving bronchodilators, and treating the cause.

questions.stem: If signs of bronchospasm persist, which mechanical causes should be excluded? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Think kinked tubing, mucous plug, right mainstem intubation, pneumothorax, or circuit obstruction.

questions.stem: Refer to the ventilator trend. Peak pressure jumps from 20 to 42 and Vt falls at minute 3. What should you check FIRST?
options: Patient and airway: breath sounds, tube, kinks
Replace the CO2 absorbent and recheck the pressures
Give a fluid bolus for low tidal volume
questions.explanation: Start with the patient and airway: assess breath sounds, tube position, and obstruction before blaming equipment.

questions.stem: Refer to the ventilator trend. Breath sounds are absent on the left after a laparoscopic trocar placement near the diaphragm. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.explanation: Unilateral absent breath sounds with sudden high pressure after surgical manipulation suggests pneumothorax.

questions.stem: During a case with an LMA, you hear noisy, croupy inspiratory sounds and see rising airway pressures. What should you suspect?
options: Bronchospasm or laryngospasm presenting through the LMA
A normal LMA leak with no airway problem
Bubbling from secretions with no obstruction
A high-pitched whistle from a circuit leak at the Y-piece
questions.explanation: With an LMA, bronchospasm can sound croup-like. Evaluate depth and airway reactivity.

questions.stem: During a spine fusion, which findings suggest hemorrhage? (Select 3)
options: Increased pulse pressure or stroke volume variation
Saturated laps and blood in the canister
questions.explanation: Hemorrhage causes hypotension, tachycardia, rising PPV or SVV, and visible blood loss.

questions.stem: During a liver resection, the surgeon reports a torn hepatic vein and suction canisters fill rapidly. What is your FIRST set of actions?
options: Call for help, give 100% FiO2, and open fluids
Give a vasopressor and wait for labs
Give a beta-blocker to slow the heart
questions.explanation: Major hemorrhage calls for help, 100% FiO2, open fluids, large-bore access, vasopressors, blood products, and invasive monitoring.

questions.stem: During a long orthopedic case, BP drifts down and HR rises, but the surgeon reports minimal bleeding. What should you do?
options: Walk around and check laps, the floor, and canisters
Verify the sponge count with the circulator
Check that the drapes are sterile
questions.explanation: Blood loss is often gradual and hidden. Look at saturated laps, blood on the floor, and canister levels.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for a revision hip arthroplasty with expected large blood loss. What IV access is BEST?
questions.explanation: Two large-bore IVs allow rapid volume and blood administration.

questions.stem: At the end of a long abdominal case, the esophageal temperature reads 35.4 °C. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: Hypothermia is a core temperature below 36 °C.

questions.stem: A patient's core temperature is 34.8 °C at the end of a 5-hour case. Which complications should you anticipate? (Select 4)
options: Bleeding from impaired platelets and clotting
questions.explanation: Hypothermia causes coagulopathy, infection, slow drug clearance, cardiac stress, and shivering.

questions.stem: In PACU, a hypothermic 72-year-old with CAD is shivering violently and develops ST depression. What links the two?
questions.explanation: Shivering can increase oxygen consumption several-fold, raising myocardial demand in patients with CAD.

questions.stem: A patient's core temperature was 34.8 °C for most of a colectomy, and she later develops a wound infection. What mechanism links these?
questions.explanation: Hypothermia causes vasoconstriction and reduced tissue oxygen and impairs white cell function, raising infection risk.

questions.stem: A hypothermic patient (34.5 °C) remains weak and sedated an hour after a case despite standard doses. What explains this?
options: Drug metabolism slows, prolonging drug effects
The patient received too little reversal
questions.explanation: Hypothermia slows drug metabolism and prolongs NMB and sedative effects.

questions.stem: A patient's temperature is 35.2 °C near closure. Which emergence effect is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Hypothermia slows metabolism and delays emergence.

questions.stem: Case 1: Ten minutes after incision, BP falls from 125/75 to 72/38, HR 92, ETCO2 unchanged, no obvious bleeding. What is the FIRST step?
options: Confirm BP accuracy, then evaluate the mechanism
Give a unit of blood immediately for suspected bleeding
questions.explanation: Start by confirming the reading, then consider vasodilation, depth, medications, and occult bleeding.

questions.stem: Case 1: The BP is confirmed low. Volatile is at 1.3 MAC and a large bolus of fentanyl was just given. What is the MOST likely mechanism?
questions.explanation: Excess anesthetic depth after a stimulus peak often causes vasodilation; reduce depth and support BP.

questions.stem: Which clinical sign during hemorrhage suggests fluid responsiveness?
questions.explanation: PPV/SVV increase with hypovolemia and suggest fluid responsiveness.

questions.stem: During ongoing hemorrhage in a vascular case, you need frequent labs and beat-to-beat BP. What is the key next step?
options: Stop all fluids to avoid dilution
Lower FiO2 to limit oxygen toxicity
questions.explanation: An arterial line gives continuous BP and allows frequent labs to guide resuscitation.

questions.stem: A patient becomes hypotensive after a tourniquet is released. Which mechanism is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Tourniquet release causes reperfusion and vasodilation, lowering BP.

questions.stem: A hypothermic patient bleeds more than expected and develops chest pain in PACU. Which effects of hypothermia explain this? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Hypothermia impairs platelets and coagulation and increases myocardial oxygen demand through shivering.

questions.stem: Three patients receive desflurane, sevoflurane, and isoflurane at 1 MAC for identical cases. Which agent will allow the fastest emergence, and why?
options: Sevoflurane, because it is the least pungent
Isoflurane, because it is the most potent
questions.explanation: Desflurane's low blood-gas solubility gives the fastest onset and recovery.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: You are running sevoflurane in a healthy 40-year-old. What end-tidal concentration is about 1 MAC?
questions.explanation: Sevoflurane MAC is about 2.0%, isoflurane about 1.15%, and desflurane about 6.0%.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: You switch a patient to desflurane. What end-tidal concentration is about 1 MAC?
questions.explanation: Desflurane MAC is about 6.0%.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A patient is maintained on isoflurane. What end-tidal concentration is about 1 MAC?
questions.explanation: Isoflurane MAC is about 1.15%.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: During maintenance, desflurane is abruptly increased from 6% to 12%. HR rises to 125 and BP to 170/95. What explains this?
options: Light anesthesia from the change in agent
questions.explanation: Rapid increases in desflurane can cause sympathetic stimulation and airway irritation.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A child with asthma needs a mask induction. Which agent fits BEST?
questions.explanation: Sevoflurane is non-pungent and a bronchodilator, making it ideal for inhalation induction.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Two identical patients receive isoflurane and sevoflurane for 3-hour cases. The isoflurane patient takes longer to wake. Why?
questions.explanation: Isoflurane's higher solubility slows emergence compared with sevoflurane and desflurane.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A 30-year-old and an 80-year-old both receive sevoflurane at 2.0%. Which patient is MORE likely to become hypotensive, and why?
options: The 80-year-old, because MAC decreases with age
The 30-year-old, because MAC increases with age
Both equally, since MAC is constant
Neither, since 2.0% equals 1 MAC at any age
questions.explanation: MAC decreases about 6% per decade after 40, so 2.0% is well over 1 MAC for an 80-year-old.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: During maintenance with desflurane, which fresh gas flow meets the ASA low-flow quality measure?
questions.explanation: For desflurane and isoflurane, low flow means 1 L/min or less.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: During maintenance with sevoflurane, which fresh gas flow meets the ASA low-flow quality measure?
questions.explanation: Sevoflurane is allowed up to 2 L/min under the low-flow measure.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Your department is adopting a low-flow anesthesia policy. Which benefits support it? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Low-flow anesthesia lowers agent use, cost, waste, and emissions. Depth changes more slowly and gas monitoring matters more.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: You are running sevoflurane at 1 L/min and need to rapidly deepen for incision. What adjustment is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Higher fresh gas flow speeds changes in circuit concentration; it is appropriate at induction or when rapid changes are needed.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Which cases favor TIVA during maintenance? (Select 2)
options: Need for rapid emergence after a 10-minute case
Short cases with no PONV risk only
Short outpatient cases with no PONV history
questions.explanation: TIVA is favored for neuromonitoring and significant PONV history, as well as MH susceptibility and some geriatric patients.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with mild cognitive impairment is scheduled for a hip fracture repair under GA. Why might TIVA be chosen?
options: Older patients clear propofol faster than volatile agents
It avoids hypotension better than volatiles
It removes the need for processed EEG
questions.explanation: TIVA has been associated with reduced postoperative delirium and cognitive dysfunction in older patients.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: You plan TIVA for a spine case with neuromonitoring. Which drugs are commonly used? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: TIVA uses IV agents such as propofol, remifentanil, ketamine, lidocaine, and dexmedetomidine.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: You are setting up TIVA for a 6-hour spine case. Which safety steps are essential? (Select 4)
options: Enough drug drawn up or available for the full case
The pump on emergency power with a charged battery
Minimal dead space with visible connections
Gravity drips in place of pumps
No further IV checks after induction
questions.explanation: TIVA safety includes adequate drug supply, power and battery, correct programming, IV patency, visible connections, minimal dead space, and a backup plan.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Halfway through a TIVA case, the propofol syringe runs out and pharmacy is slow to restock. What principle would have prevented a gap in anesthesia?
options: Always have a backup plan and enough drug
Avoid pumps entirely to reduce programming errors
questions.explanation: TIVA requires enough drug for the case and a backup plan, such as a volatile agent, if delivery fails.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Case 9: BP and HR rise, and BIS increases. You discover the TIVA infusion is not being delivered. What is the FIRST action?
options: Restore anesthesia immediately with a bolus or volatile
Increase the infusion rate on the same line
questions.explanation: Restore anesthesia immediately, then troubleshoot delivery and address possible awareness.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A paralyzed patient becomes light during a case. Why might you not notice?
options: NMB removes movement as a warning sign
questions.explanation: Paralysis removes movement, an important clinical sign of light anesthesia.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: During TIVA, which monitor helps confirm adequate hypnosis since you cannot measure end-tidal agent?
questions.explanation: Processed EEG is especially useful when end-tidal agent monitoring is unavailable, as in TIVA.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: An 85-year-old with dementia has a BIS of 32 at 0.6 MAC, and a nearby cautery causes BIS spikes. How should you interpret these values?
options: A low BIS means excessive depth in every patient
BIS is accurate across ages and drugs
questions.explanation: Processed EEG values must be interpreted with age, drugs, artifact, and neurologic state in mind.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: You can give fentanyl as repeated boluses or as an infusion during a long case. What advantage does a continuous infusion offer?
options: Stable plasma levels with a lower total dose
questions.explanation: Infusions avoid peaks and troughs, giving stable levels and often a lower total dose.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A remifentanil infusion needs very precise delivery at a low rate. Which device is MOST precise?
questions.explanation: Syringe pumps provide the most precise delivery for potent infusions.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Your ambulatory center adopts opioid-sparing ERAS for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Which benefits might you see? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Opioid-sparing pathways shorten discharge, reduce unplanned admissions, and lower PACU opioid use. Long-term benefit is less certain.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: You are building an opioid-sparing plan for a laparoscopic colectomy. Which nonopioid adjuncts fit? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Multimodal adjuncts include NSAIDs, acetaminophen, ketamine, magnesium, lidocaine, and regional blocks.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Your group is rolling out opioid-sparing anesthesia. Which challenges should you expect? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Challenges include block skill demands, collaboration across teams, ongoing opioid use after discharge, and uncertain long-term benefit.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: During a sevoflurane anesthetic in an 82-year-old receiving dexmedetomidine, you assess depth. Which questions apply? (Select 3)
options: Is the correct agent running with adequate supply?
Are inspired and end-tidal concentrations reviewed?
Is MAC adjusted for age and adjuncts?
Is the vaporizer set to 1 MAC regardless of patient?
Is the BIS turned off to reduce alarms?
Is the surgeon satisfied with the depth?
questions.explanation: Depth assessment checks agent and supply, inspired and end-tidal concentrations, MAC adjusted for age and adjuncts, and clinical context.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: At the end of a case, you need to confirm full neuromuscular recovery before extubation. Which monitoring site is preferred?
options: Ulnar nerve at the adductor pollicis
Facial nerve at the orbicularis oculi
Posterior tibial nerve at the flexor hallucis
Facial nerve at the corrugator supercilii
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve and adductor pollicis are preferred for assessing recovery.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Both arms are tucked for a prone spine case. Which TOF site can you use instead?
options: Facial nerve at the orbicularis oculi
Ulnar nerve at the adductor pollicis
Median nerve at the thenar eminence
Radial nerve at the wrist extensors
questions.explanation: The facial nerve site is an alternative when arms are tucked and better reflects onset.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: You monitor the facial nerve during induction and the ulnar nerve before extubation. Which phrase captures why?
options: Facial nerve for onset; thumb for recovery
Thumb for onset; facial nerve for recovery
Facial nerve for both onset and recovery
questions.explanation: The facial nerve reflects onset and depth; the adductor pollicis best reflects recovery.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: You redosed rocuronium 40 minutes ago during a long laparoscopy. How often should TOF be checked during maintenance?
options: About every 15 minutes and around redosing or reversal
At the end of the case before giving any reversal
questions.explanation: Check TOF about every 15 minutes, and before and after redosing NMBs or giving reversal.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: During a long case, TOF returns to 2 twitches and the surgeon needs relaxation for another hour. What rocuronium redose is appropriate for a 70 kg patient?
questions.explanation: Rocuronium redosing is about 0.1–0.2 mg/kg, or 7–14 mg for 70 kg.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: The surgeon says the abdomen "feels tight," and you plan to judge relaxation. Which monitoring method is the standard?
options: Quantitative monitoring with a numeric TOF ratio
Clinical signs such as head lift
The surgeon's feedback on abdominal wall relaxation
questions.explanation: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring is the standard because qualitative assessment misses residual block.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: TOF is 2 twitches during a laparoscopy, and you are about to redose rocuronium. What should you do first?
options: Ask the surgeon how close they are to finishing
Redose every 30 minutes to keep zero twitches
questions.explanation: Ask whether the case is ending before redosing, to avoid deep block at emergence.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Refer to the TOF figure. Patient 1 has a TOFR of 0.65, Patient 2 has 0.95, and Patient 3 has two twitches. Which patient is ready for extubation from a neuromuscular standpoint?
questions.explanation: A TOF ratio above 0.9 indicates adequate recovery; 0.65 and two twitches indicate residual block.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Refer to the TOF figure. Patient 1's fourth twitch is 13 mm high and the first is 20 mm. What is the TOFR, and what should you do?
questions.explanation: TOFR = T4/T1 = 13/20 = 0.65. Below 0.9 is residual block, so give more reversal and recheck.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: During a hip revision, a stable patient's hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL. What is the BEST action?
options: Give crystalloid and recheck in 30 minutes
questions.explanation: A hemoglobin below 7 g/dL prompts consideration of PRBC transfusion.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: During a colectomy, hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL with stable vitals and normal lactate. How should you decide on transfusion?
options: Assess the patient and clinical context, not just the number
Transfuse to keep Hgb above 10 g/dL
Give iron and recheck in PACU
Wait until it falls below 5 g/dL
questions.explanation: For hemoglobin 7–10 g/dL, decisions depend on the clinical picture, ongoing loss, and oxygen delivery.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: During a laparoscopy, BP is 82/48 after you have given 2 L of crystalloid. Before giving more fluid, what should you ask?
options: Is the patient already on vasopressors?
Is the surgeon asking for fluids?
questions.explanation: Ask repeatedly whether hypotension is fluid responsive before reflexively giving more volume.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: During major hemorrhage, which derangements should be anticipated? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Massive hemorrhage and transfusion cause hypocalcemia from citrate and hypothermia, plus acidosis and dilutional coagulopathy.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: During a trauma laparotomy, the surgeon estimates 300 mL blood loss, but HR is 125 and lap sponges are soaked. How should blood loss be estimated?
options: Combine field, suction, sponges, drains, vitals, and labs
Use the surgeon's verbal estimate given at closure
questions.explanation: Blood loss is estimated from multiple sources, not one.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Which fluids are commonly used during maintenance?
questions.explanation: Balanced crystalloids are commonly used; colloid/blood depends on status and practice.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Urine output is 5 mL over the last hour during a stable case. What should you check before blaming renal hypoperfusion?
options: The catheter and tubing for obstruction or kinking
The total fluid balance and crystalloid given so far
questions.explanation: Check the catheter and tubing for obstruction before attributing low output to hypoperfusion.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Which time-dependent therapies should be tracked during maintenance? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Track antibiotics, anticoagulation, insulin, TXA, steroids, antiarrhythmics, and procedure-specific meds.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: During massive transfusion, the field oozes despite surgical control. Which tests help guide product replacement? (Select 3)
options: Viscoelastic testing such as TEG or ROTEM
questions.explanation: Coagulation is assessed with conventional and viscoelastic testing, and Hgb/Hct are trended with significant loss.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Why should type and screen be verified during maintenance?
options: Blood products may be needed for ongoing loss
It is required before every case
It confirms the patient's blood type for records
It guides neuromuscular dosing for the rest of the case
questions.explanation: Verify type/screen or crossmatch and product availability when indicated.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Which balance should opioid dosing reflect during maintenance? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Balance opioid needs against age, tolerance, OSA risk, organ function, and destination.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: A patient receives 6 L of crystalloid during a 4-hour bowel case and develops pulmonary edema. Another receives 500 mL and is oliguric with lactate rising. What principle was violated in both?
options: Maximize fluid to prevent any hypotension
questions.explanation: Fluid management aims to support perfusion without hypovolemia or overload.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Patient A has Hgb 7.5 with stable vitals and no ongoing loss. Patient B has Hgb 8.5 with HR 125, MAP 55, and active bleeding. Which is MORE likely to need transfusion?
options: Patient A, since her number is lower
questions.explanation: Transfusion decisions are individualized and not based on one threshold; ongoing loss and instability matter.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: A patient receives multiple units of blood and develops arrhythmias. Which electrolyte disturbance is MOST likely from citrate?
questions.explanation: Massive transfusion can cause hypocalcemia, which the lecture lists to anticipate.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: After you turn off the sevoflurane at the end of a case, the patient gradually begins breathing, then opens her eyes. How is emergence best described?
options: A passive return from general anesthesia
